title: Madhya Pradesh bases crop insurance claims on YES-TECH satellite and AI yield estimates; some farmers report faster payment and others lower claims
summary: YES-TECH feeds satellite and weather data to a machine-learning model whose yield estimates set crop insurance claims in Madhya Pradesh; some farmers report faster payment and others lower claims.
account: On 21 July 2023 India's Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare launched the YES-TECH manual. It covers a technology-driven yield estimation system under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY), the government crop insurance scheme. The system was piloted in 100 districts. It estimates yields at gram panchayat level for claim assessment. A Press Information Bureau (PIB) release of 17 February 2025 says that YES-TECH was introduced from kharif 2023. It blends technology-based yield estimates with manual crop-cutting experiments (CCEs). A PIB backgrounder of 14 February 2026 says that YES-TECH uses remote sensing and AI-driven analytics. It was introduced for paddy and wheat in kharif 2023 and extended to soybean in kharif 2024 with a minimum 30 percent weightage. As of January 2025 nine states had adopted it, and Madhya Pradesh had transitioned fully. The backgrounder says that this enables timely loss assessment and faster claim settlement, and it gives no figures. A Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) presentation by Chhavi Mahaur at a webinar of 18 May 2026 describes the Madhya Pradesh implementation. The Madhya Pradesh Council of Science and Technology (MPCST) runs it with the National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) in Hyderabad. Satellite and weather data are run into a machine learning model (the “AI/ML model”) for kharif and a “semi-physical model” for rabi. Insurers use the results to disburse PMFBY claims. Madhya Pradesh is the only major state that gives YES-TECH 100 percent weightage. CSE reported that twelve states were implementing YES-TECH. CSE's field assessment covered some 50 farmers in Sehore, Vidisha and Bhopal. Large soybean farmers reported lower claims than under manual CCEs, and some urged a rollback. Some farmers appreciated faster disbursement. Insurers and officials blamed the lower claims on historically under-reported manual yields. District officials told CSE that claims paid for similar crop losses had become more consistent since the technology came in. They also called the process opaque. Down To Earth reported on 20 August 2026 that kharif payouts in the three districts fell from Rs 217.91 crore to Rs 55.2 crore between 2018 and 2024. It reported that farmers and unions protested in 2024–25. No official document with a quantified beneficial outcome is among the sources.
purpose: Estimate crop yields from satellite, weather and model data to replace or supplement manual crop-cutting experiments. The aim: insurance losses assessed accurately and claims paid on time. The claimed benefit (faster, more transparent settlement) is that purpose and is contested.
system: YES-TECH (Yield Estimation System based on Technology): satellite remote sensing, weather data and analytical models, including an 'AI/ML model' for kharif crops and a 'semi-physical model' for rabi crops in Madhya Pradesh
developer: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare (YES-TECH manual); Madhya Pradesh implementation by the Madhya Pradesh Council of Science and Technology as Technology Implementation Partner, mentored by NRSC Hyderabad (per CSE)
deployer: Government of Madhya Pradesh under PMFBY with insurers (AIC, SBI General Insurance, HDFC Ergo); nine states in all as of January 2025
location: Madhya Pradesh, India (CSE field assessment in Sehore, Vidisha and Bhopal districts)
taxonomy_note: Officials claim faster claim settlement without figures, while independent sources report lower payouts and rollback demands in three districts.

ratings.reason: CSE reports that some farmers in Sehore, Vidisha and Bhopal valued faster payment of claims than before. That is time saved. Other farmers in the same districts report lower claims than their losses.

District officials told CSE that claims for similar crop losses had become more consistent since the technology came in. They gave no figures and also called the process opaque. The PIB states that settlement is faster and gives no figures.

The PIB reports adoption by nine states, and CSE later reports twelve. No source documents an outcome at scale. Down To Earth reports that payouts in three districts fell sharply between 2018 and 2024.

ai_role.statement: Official PIB documents (deployer, not the model's maker) state YES-TECH employs AI-driven analytics and that Madhya Pradesh relies fully on technology-based yield estimates. CSE's presentation says kharif yields come from an “AI/ML model” whose results are used to disburse claims. The model output thus directly determines payouts. Whether this produced a benefit is contested. PIB asserts faster, more transparent settlement without data. CSE and Down To Earth document reduced claims, protests and rollback calls among large soybean farmers in Sehore, Vidisha and Bhopal. They also record some farmers' appreciation of timeliness and insurers' claim that manual yields were under-reported. No independent quantified beneficial outcome was found.

fields.account: On 21 July 2023 India's Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare launched the YES-TECH manual. It covers a technology-driven yield estimation system under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY), the government crop insurance scheme. The system was piloted in 100 districts. It estimates yields at gram panchayat level for claim assessment. A Press Information Bureau (PIB) release of 17 February 2025 says that YES-TECH was introduced from kharif 2023. It blends technology-based yield estimates with manual crop-cutting experiments (CCEs). A PIB backgrounder of 14 February 2026 says that YES-TECH uses remote sensing and AI-driven analytics. It was introduced for paddy and wheat in kharif 2023 and extended to soybean in kharif 2024 with a minimum 30 percent weightage. As of January 2025 nine states had adopted it, and Madhya Pradesh had transitioned fully. The backgrounder says that this enables timely loss assessment and faster claim settlement, and it gives no figures. A Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) presentation by Chhavi Mahaur at a webinar of 18 May 2026 describes the Madhya Pradesh implementation. The Madhya Pradesh Council of Science and Technology (MPCST) runs it with the National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) in Hyderabad. Satellite and weather data are run into a machine learning model (the “AI/ML model”) for kharif and a “semi-physical model” for rabi. Insurers use the results to disburse PMFBY claims. Madhya Pradesh is the only major state that gives YES-TECH 100 percent weightage. CSE reported that twelve states were implementing YES-TECH. CSE's field assessment covered some 50 farmers in Sehore, Vidisha and Bhopal. Large soybean farmers reported lower claims than under manual CCEs, and some urged a rollback. Some farmers appreciated faster disbursement. Insurers and officials blamed the lower claims on historically under-reported manual yields. District officials told CSE that claims paid for similar crop losses had become more consistent since the technology came in. They also called the process opaque. Down To Earth reported on 20 August 2026 that kharif payouts in the three districts fell from Rs 217.91 crore to Rs 55.2 crore between 2018 and 2024. It reported that farmers and unions protested in 2024–25. No official document with a quantified beneficial outcome is among the sources.
